content: The cover design features a delicate, smoky background image that symbolizes the well-documented health risks associated with smoke from combustible tobacco products. It also highlights the less-studied emissions from electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS), such as e-cigarettes, which release misty aerosols containing nicotine and other substances. This imagery underscores the importance of addressing both traditional tobacco smoke and emissions from vaping devices in workplace health policies. The text box on the cover references the NIOSH Total Worker Health™ strategy, which emphasizes protecting workers from occupational hazards, including exposure to secondhand tobacco smoke (SHS) in the workplace. This strategy also promotes workplace health initiatives targeting lifestyle risk factors, such as tobacco use among employees. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) issues Current Intelligence Bulletins (CIBs) to disseminate new scientific information about occupational hazards. These bulletins may highlight previously unrecognized risks, report new data on known hazards, or provide guidance on hazard control. Despite decades of public health efforts to reduce tobacco-related disease and death, significant work remains to achieve a tobacco-free society. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), of which NIOSH is a part, has identified reducing tobacco use as a Winnable Battle. Marking the 50th anniversary of the first Surgeon General's report on the health consequences of smoking, NIOSH has released CIB 67, titled Promoting Health and Preventing Disease and Injury through Workplace Tobacco Policies. This bulletin addresses the risks faced by workers who use tobacco products or are exposed to SHS in workplaces where smoking is permitted. Tobacco smoke contains carcinogenic and toxic components, and while cigarette smoking has declined, millions of workers still smoke, and many workplaces continue to allow smoking. Other forms of tobacco, such as smokeless tobacco, also pose health risks to users. Tobacco use in the workplace not only directly harms the health of users and those exposed to SHS but can also exacerbate the effects of other occupational hazards. For example, workplace chemicals may interact with tobacco smoke, increasing toxicity and health risks. Contaminated tobacco products can introduce toxic agents into the body, and the combined effects of tobacco use and workplace exposures can significantly amplify the risk of occupational diseases, such as lung cancer in asbestos-exposed workers who smoke. CIB 67 outlines several key aspects of tobacco use in the workplace, including: Tobacco use prevalence among workers. SHS exposure in workplaces. Occupational health and safety concerns related to tobacco use. Existing regulations and recommendations limiting tobacco use in workplaces. Hazards of SHS exposure in the workplace. Interventions to eliminate or reduce these hazards. NIOSH recommends that employers establish and maintain smoke-free workplaces to protect employees from involuntary exposure to tobacco smoke and emissions from ENDS. Ideally, these policies should be paired with comprehensive tobacco cessation support programs. Employers should also comply with OSHA and MSHA regulations that prohibit or limit smoking in areas with explosive, flammable, or toxic materials. Employers are encouraged to inform workers about the health risks of tobacco use and SHS exposure, provide training on the increased risks of combining tobacco use with occupational hazards, and offer resources such as quitlines, mobile interventions, and web-based cessation programs. Comprehensive cessation programs should be made available at no cost, particularly for lower-wage workers, and health insurance plans should cover evidence-based cessation treatments without financial barriers. NIOSH also advises workers who use tobacco to comply with workplace tobacco policies, seek employer-provided cessation resources, and quit using tobacco products. Quitting tobacco use is beneficial at any age, and evidence-based treatments can significantly increase the likelihood of successful cessation. The scientific foundation for recognizing tobacco use as the leading preventable cause of premature death and disease in the United States is robust. Since the first Surgeon General's report in 1964, subsequent reports have documented the serious health consequences of active smoking, SHS exposure, and smokeless tobacco use. These include cancer, heart disease, and respiratory diseases. Effective smoking cessation programs and workplace policies have been shown to reduce tobacco use prevalence, improve worker health, and decrease tobacco-related morbidity and mortality. NIOSH emphasizes that eliminating tobacco use in the workplace is the most effective way to reduce SHS exposure and improve worker health. Employers are encouraged to adopt participatory approaches when developing tobacco-related policies, considering input from employees, labor representatives, and occupational health professionals. Differential employment benefits or hiring policies based on tobacco use should be carefully evaluated for ethical concerns and unintended consequences.
